analysis.one_liner: Exempts traditional premium cigars from FDA health regulation and tobacco user fees.
analysis.headline: A bill to exempt premium cigars from FDA oversight drew 167 cosponsors (28 Democrats, 139 Republicans) but never got a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written premium cigars — handmade, all-leaf-tobacco cigars — permanently out of the Food and Drug Administration's authority under the tobacco-control law, and out of the user fees tobacco companies pay to fund FDA oversight. That means no FDA health warnings, product standards, or testing requirements for premium cigars, and no fees on the industry to pay for tobacco regulation. The bill was introduced in February 2013, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received so much as a subcommittee vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Premium cigar manufacturers, importers, distributors, and the small retail shops that sell them. They would be permanently shielded from FDA product oversight and from the user fees that other tobacco products pay to fund the FDA's tobacco program. Because the exemption is written into the statute itself, no future administration could reverse it through regulation.

how_it_helps.text: Hand-rolled premium cigar makers and their suppliers would avoid FDA product standards, premarket review, and mandatory health warnings on packaging and advertising.
The bill amends the user-fee provisions of the tobacco law so that premium cigars would not be assessed FDA tobacco user fees, saving the industry money that other tobacco product makers pay.

The exemption is defined to cover only traditional large and premium cigars — 100% leaf tobacco, no filter, hand-rolled or laid by hand on a single machine — while excluding cigarettes and little cigars, so the carve-out is narrow by design.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers of premium cigars, who would buy a tobacco product with no FDA health warnings, ingredient disclosure, or product testing, and the public more broadly, since an entire category of tobacco products would sit permanently outside federal health oversight. The FDA's tobacco program would also forgo fee revenue from this segment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cigar consumers and public health oversight

drawbacks.text: Premium cigars are not risk-free: cigar smoke contains the same cancer-causing compounds as other tobacco products, and the exemption would leave a tobacco category with no federal requirement for health warnings, ingredient testing, or youth-access enforcement.

Writing the exemption into statute, rather than leaving it to regulators, would prevent FDA from ever covering premium cigars even if later evidence showed a significant public health problem in the category.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a clear, permanent financial and regulatory benefit to one tobacco industry segment — no fees, no warnings, no product oversight — while the cost falls diffusely on consumers who lose health protections and on the public-health system. The honest case for it is economic: hand-rolled cigars are a niche craft product made by small businesses, and FDA fees and rules could burden shops and jobs. But the bill does not just limit rules; it categorically removes FDA authority over a tobacco product forever, which is a poor trade for the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for nearly two years without a markup or vote, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Representative Bill Posey of Florida introduced the bill on February 15, 2013, with 13 original cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Health, which is where the action history ends.
The bill attracted 167 cosponsors — 28 Democrats and 139 Republicans — but the committee never reported it, and it never received a floor vote.
All bills die automatically when a Congress ends, so the bill lapsed in January 2015 with no vote ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, premium cigars were not carved out of the tobacco-control law and FDA's authority over cigars was left intact. Consumers and public health interests came out ahead; the cigar industry did not get its exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public health, since FDA kept cigar authority

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt premium cigars from FDA regulation and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 167 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one of the larger cosponsor lists of any tobacco bill in the Congress, though many members of tobacco-state and cigar-district delegations.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (and its Health Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 15, 2013 and never held a markup or voted the bill out; the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Public health groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed carving any tobacco products, including premium cigars, out of FDA oversight.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but skewed Republican: 139 of the 167 cosponsors were Republicans and 28 were Democrats, and the lead sponsor was a Republican from Florida, a major cigar state.

industries.note: The bill would exempt their products from FDA tobacco regulation and user fees permanently, by statute. The industry's gain — freedom from health warnings, product standards, and fees — comes directly at the cost of consumer health protections on a tobacco product.

Small tobacconists and lounge operators would be spared the compliance and fee costs of FDA oversight, which the bill's supporters argued threatened small businesses and hand-rolling jobs. Their benefit is the removal of consumer-facing regulation rather than a lower price or better product for buyers.

industries.industry: Cigarette and other tobacco product makers
industries.note: They remain fully regulated and fee-assessed, but a competitor category would gain a regulatory and cost advantage they do not have.
